newsitem.title: USA: Hoarse Clinton says law must not hurt children.
newsitem.headline: Hoarse Clinton says law must not hurt children.

text.p: Struggling to speak with a hoarse voice, President Clinton said Saturday that a welfare law he signed should not be allowed to penalize children.

"Now that we have ended welfare as we know it, let the change not be to have even more children in more abject poverty, but to move people who can work into jobs," Clinton said in his weekly radio address, delivered from the presidential retreat at Camp David, Maryland.
Clinton has drawn fire from fellow Democrats for signing a welfare law Aug. 22 that, among other things, ends a 61-year guarantee of federal aid for the country's poorest children.
Aid to Families with Dependent Children, the main federal cash welfare program, and smaller programs are folded into an annual block grant to states to run their own programs instead.

The president has pledged to seek amendments to the law next year to correct what he calls its "serious flaws," although Republicans who pushed Clinton to sign it have given no indications they want any changes.
Clinton included his welfare remarks in a radio address devoted to celebrating the spirit of Thanksgiving, the holiday celebrated with feasting Thursday.

"The spirit of family and faith and community that shines so brilliantly on Thanksgiving can enable us to meet every challenge before us all year long," he said. "So let us resolve to go forward together to lift millions of people from welfare and dependency into lives of dignity and independence."

In response to Clinton's address, Republican Rep. J.C. Watts of Oklahoma described the President's signature of the welfare law as a step "to end the crippling cycle of dependency" for many Americans grown too reliant on services and entitlements.
He urged that smaller government be coupled with more reliance on giving and compassion.

"As we ask the government to do less, each of us must do more," Watts said. "Fewer dollars spent and fewer decisions made in Washington give us the opportunity to make more choices for our families, our neighborhoods, and our cities."
Clinton became hoarse on his just-completed tour of Australia and Asia. He is drinking tea, taking lozenges and under doctor's orders to rest his voice.
He was to have recorded his radio address Friday for Saturday broadcast, but decided to do it live Saturday to give his voice an extra day's rest, officials said. He returns to Washington Sunday.
White House aides are currently studying options for amending the welfare law to be included in Clinton's budget proposal for the next fiscal year, to be presented in February.

"When he signed the welfare reform bill he specifically cited concerns about provisions relating to nutrition and to the denial of benefits to legal immigrants, especially those who have worked and played by the rules," a White House spokesman, Barry Toiv, said. "As he puts his budget together he is looking at possible ways of addressing those concerns."
Critics accuse Clinton of hypocrisy for complaining about the law after signing it.

"The president, having zigged when he signed the bill, now zags and offers himself as the champion of some of the very people that the bill will squeeze," the Washington Post said in an editorial Friday.

The welfare law is to make more than $50 billion in spending cuts over the next six years. The White House has tried to cast doubt on a New York Times report that Clinton wants to restore one quarter of the savings.

Clinton is under pressure to amend the welfare law. His wife, Hillary, recently expressed a desire for a "formal role" in shaping policy on welfare reform, but the White House played down her remarks.

Three top officials of the Health and Human Services Department resigned in August in outrage over Clinton's decision to sign the bill, saying it would throw at least a million more children into poverty.
The New York Times estimated Saturday that last year about 14.7 million children fell into the "poor" category, 20.8 percent of all children in America.
